title: Sun Safety: Shade First for the Littlest
hook: Baby skin burns fast and shows damage for life. Under 6 months the rule is shade and clothing, not sunscreen; after that, sunscreen joins the hat and shade — not replaces them.
key_points: Under 6 months: keep babies out of direct sun. Use shade, a wide-brimmed hat, and lightweight clothing that covers arms and legs.
For babies under 6 months, use a little sunscreen only on small areas (face, backs of hands) when shade and clothing aren't enough.
From 6 months on, apply broad-spectrum SPF 15–50, reapply every 2 hours and after swimming — alongside, not instead of, shade and hats.
Heat is a danger too: dress light, offer extra fluids, and avoid the strongest midday sun.
content_html: A baby's skin is thin and burns quickly, and early sunburns add up to real damage over a lifetime. The advice changes with age. For babies under six months, the safest approach is to keep them out of direct sun altogether: seek shade, dress them in lightweight clothes that cover arms and legs, and add a wide-brimmed hat. If shade and clothing genuinely aren't enough, the AAP says it's fine to use a small amount of sunscreen on exposed areas like the face and the backs of the hands.
extra_html: From six months on, sunscreen becomes a regular tool — a broad-spectrum product around SPF 15 to 50, applied generously and reapplied every two hours and after swimming or sweating. The important mindset is that sunscreen adds to shade, hats, and clothing rather than replacing them. Don't forget heat: babies overheat easily, so dress them lightly, offer extra fluids in warm weather, and steer clear of the most intense midday sun. This is general guidance — ask your pediatrician about sun protection for your baby's age and skin.

related.title: Water Safety
related.hook: Drowning is fast and silent — no splashing, no shouting. The single best protection for a young child is an adult within arm's reach whenever there's water.

related.title: Childproofing the Home
related.hook: Anchoring furniture and TVs is the childproofing step parents skip most — and tip-overs are one of the deadliest home hazards for young kids. Then you cover the rest and redo it as baby gets mobile.

flashcards.prompt: What's the main way to protect a baby under 6 months from the sun?

choices.text: Shade, a wide-brimmed hat, and lightweight covering clothing
A thick layer of sunscreen all over their body
Letting them tan gradually to build tolerance

flashcards.explanation_html: For babies under 6 months the AAP advises keeping them out of direct sun, using shade, hats, and clothing — with only a little sunscreen on small areas if needed.

flashcards.prompt: Once a child is over 6 months, does sunscreen replace shade and hats?
flashcards.back_html: No — it joins them. Use broad-spectrum SPF 15–50, reapply every 2 hours and after swimming, and still rely on shade, hats, and clothing. Watch for overheating too.
